ECE 6390

Carrier phase and frequency offset

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows a known pilot that starts on the I axis and turns 90° in 0.25 ms when the receiver reference runs 1 kHz above the transmitter, beside a QPSK constellation turned by a fixed 30° phase error.

A coherent receiver multiplies the received carrier by its own reference and filters to obtain I and Q. If the reference leads the transmitter by a phase ε, every recovered point is multiplied by e^(−jε): the whole constellation turns clockwise by ε. A constant ε is a fixed rotation that one correction removes.

With a frequency difference Δf = f_LO − f_c in hertz, the phase error grows as ε(t) = ε₀ + 2πΔf t. The constellation keeps turning at 360Δf degrees per second, or 360Δf/Rs degrees per symbol at symbol rate Rs. A one-part-per-million error at a 1 GHz carrier is already 1 kHz, enough to turn the points 90° in a quarter millisecond.

QPSK decides by quadrant, so a noise-free point crosses a decision boundary once |ε| reaches 45°; noise makes errors begin sooner. A known header lets the receiver estimate ε₀ and Δf and multiply by the inverse rotation. Residual frequency error and oscillator phase noise still require phase tracking through the packet.

Carrier recovery and symbol timing are separate tasks. Carrier phase rotates the I/Q coordinates; symbol timing chooses where along each pulse to sample. Correcting one leaves the other to be done.

Example

At Rs = 100 ksym/s and Δf = 1 kHz, the phase slips 3.6° per symbol. Starting from ε₀ = 0, the error passes 45° after 12.5 symbol intervals, so without noise symbol 13 is the first wrong QPSK decision.

Practice

1. A 2.4 GHz receiver’s reference is off by 5 ppm. What carrier frequency error results, and how long does a 90° slip take?

Multiply the carrier by 5 × 10⁻⁶, then solve 90° = 360°·Δf·t.

Δf = 12 kHz. A 90° slip takes t = 0.25/12,000 s ≈ 20.8 µs.

2. Why can one phase correction at the packet start fail to keep QPSK decisions correct when Δf ≠ 0?

Compare a fixed rotation with a rotation that grows with time.

One correction removes only ε₀. The 2πΔf t term keeps growing, so the points drift toward the quadrant boundaries; the receiver must also estimate and remove the frequency offset or track the phase.
